1. Overview & Methodology

Objective

This analysis systematically evaluates iEEG signal quality across all available minipig recording sessions. The goal is to identify which channels carry genuine neural responses to acoustic stimulation, and which are "dead" or dominated by noise. The protocol follows the experimental plan laid out in SNR_EXP.md.

Dataset

7 Subjects (sub-01 to sub-07)
41 Recording Sessions
736 Total ECoG Channels
2–32 Channels per Session

Preprocessing Pipeline

For each session, the analysis proceeds through the following steps:

  1. Load session data from processed .h5 files via torch_brain.data.Data.
  2. Extract epochs: For each stimulus trial, cut a 0.5 s rest window (immediately before) and a 0.5 s stimulus window aligned to stimulus onset. Only ECoG channels are retained.
  3. Baseline correction: For every epoch and channel, subtract the mean of the rest window from both the rest and stimulus segments. This removes slow drifts and per-trial DC offsets.
  4. Broadband filtering: Apply a 1–300 Hz 4th-order Butterworth bandpass followed by a 50 Hz notch filter (zero-phase via filtfilt).
  5. High-gamma filtering: Apply a 70–150 Hz 4th-order Butterworth bandpass (zero-phase).

SNR Metric Definition

The core metric is the Evoked-Potential SNR, computed per channel c:

SNRevoked, c = Var(&Sbar;c(t)) / [ (1/N) ∑i=1..N Var(Ri,c(t)) ]

What this formula measures

The idea is to compare how much consistent, repeatable stimulus-driven activity a channel shows versus how much random fluctuation it exhibits during silence. It does this in two steps:

  1. Numerator — signal strength (ERP variance): For each trial i, we have a 0.5 s stimulus waveform Si,c(t). We average these across all N trials to get the Event-Related Potential (ERP): &Sbar;c(t) = (1/N) ∑ Si,c(t). Trial-averaging cancels out random noise (which varies from trial to trial) and preserves any consistent time-locked neural response. We then take Var(&Sbar;c(t)) — the temporal variance of this averaged waveform. If the channel carries a genuine evoked potential, the ERP will have clear deflections and high variance. If it is pure noise, averaging drives the waveform toward a flat line with near-zero variance.
  2. Denominator — noise floor (mean rest variance): For each trial, we also have a matched 0.5 s rest window Ri,c(t) from the silence period immediately before the stimulus. We compute the temporal variance of each individual rest segment Var(Ri,c(t)) and then average these across all N trials. This gives the typical amount of moment-to-moment fluctuation the channel exhibits when no stimulus is present — i.e. the noise floor. Note that we do not average the rest waveforms before computing variance (unlike the numerator). Each rest segment is measured individually, and the variances are averaged, so this captures the characteristic noise power of the channel rather than any repeatable pattern.

Interpretation

The ratio tells us how much the consistent stimulus response “stands out” above the channel’s intrinsic noise:

  • SNR > 1: The repeatable evoked signal has more energy than a typical noise segment — a strong, clearly detectable auditory response.
  • SNR ≈ 0.5: The evoked response is about half the noise power. Still detectable but weaker.
  • SNR ≈ 0: The trial-averaged stimulus waveform is essentially flat. The channel shows no consistent time-locked response to acoustic stimulation — it is either dominated by noise, disconnected, or not in an auditory-responsive area.

Channels with SNR > 0.5 are classified as Active; the rest as Dead. This threshold was chosen as a practical cutoff: it requires the evoked response to carry at least half the energy of a typical noise segment, ensuring the channel has a meaningfully detectable stimulus-locked signal.

Why this design?

Using trial-averaged variance in the numerator but single-trial variance in the denominator is deliberate. Averaging across trials in the numerator acts as a matched filter for repeatable, stimulus-locked activity: genuine neural responses sum coherently while random noise cancels. The denominator remains unaveraged so it reflects the true per-trial noise power rather than an artificially suppressed value. This asymmetry is what gives the metric its sensitivity — a channel with a weak but reliable evoked potential will accumulate signal in the numerator while the denominator stays at the raw noise level.

2. RQ1: Channel-Level vs. Session-Level SNR

Can we establish a baseline-corrected SNR to identify dead channels and aggregate valid channels into a reliable session score?

Results

719 Dead Channels (97.7%)
17 Active Channels (2.3%)
0.0198 Median BB SNR (all)
0.76 Mean Active SNR

Distribution of Broadband SNR

The vast majority of channels have very low SNR values. The distribution is extremely right-skewed: the 90th percentile is only 0.15, and the 95th percentile is 0.35. Only 17 out of 736 channels (2.3%) exceed the 0.5 threshold.

Percentile 10th 25th 50th 75th 90th 95th 99th
BB SNR 0.0015 0.0054 0.0198 0.0472 0.1498 0.3513 0.6154

Sessions with Active Channels

Only 5 out of 41 sessions (12.2%) contain at least one active channel:

Session Active / Total Mean Active SNR Mean Active Resp. Ratio
sub-03_ses-04 LHanest 6 / 24 0.5932 0.6998

sub-07_ses-03 LH 6 / 18 0.8933 0.7570
Key Finding: The overwhelming majority of channels (97.7%) are classified as Dead at the 0.5 SNR threshold. This indicates that most electrodes in this dataset do not reliably capture evoked neural activity above their noise floor when assessed with broadband evoked-potential SNR. The few active channels tend to cluster within specific sessions and subjects (sub-03, sub-04, sub-07), suggesting that signal quality is highly dependent on surgical placement and recording conditions.

3. RQ2: High-Gamma Sensitivity Check

Does evaluating signal quality in the high-gamma band (70–150 Hz) isolate neural signals better than broadband data?

Results

0.0024 Mean HG SNR (all channels)
0.0010 Median HG SNR (all channels)
0.0048 Max HG SNR
0 Channels above 0.5 in HG

SNR Difference: High-Gamma minus Broadband

For active channels, the high-gamma SNR is dramatically lower than the broadband SNR, with a mean difference of −0.74. Even the best active channel (CG2D2E1, sub-04) drops from BB SNR = 1.54 to HG SNR = 0.007.

For dead channels, the difference is much smaller (mean −0.046), since both metrics are already near zero.

Channel Group Mean BB SNR Mean HG SNR Mean Difference
Active (17 channels) 0.7598 0.0044 −0.7403
Dead (719 channels) 0.0480 0.0023 −0.0460
Key Finding — Hypothesis Not Supported: Contrary to the hypothesis, high-gamma filtering does not improve the SNR of responsive channels. Instead, it collapses the SNR of all channels to near-zero values. No channel reaches the 0.5 threshold in the high-gamma band. This suggests that the auditory evoked responses in these minipig recordings are primarily carried by low-frequency components (ERP morphology in the broadband signal), rather than by high-gamma power modulations. The high-gamma band contains very little stimulus-locked energy relative to the background noise floor.
Interpretation: While the SNR of active channels drops massively under high-gamma filtering, the correlation between broadband and high-gamma SNR across active channels is still positive (Pearson r = 0.585, p = 0.014), meaning channels that are relatively better in broadband tend to also be relatively better in high-gamma. However, the absolute magnitudes are far too low for high-gamma SNR to serve as a useful quality metric in this dataset.

4. RQ3: Trial-by-Trial Reliability (Responsive Ratio)

What proportion of trials show a reliable energy increase during stimulus compared to baseline?

Results

72.9% Mean Resp. Ratio (Active)
47.0% Mean Resp. Ratio (Dead)
72.8% Median Resp. Ratio (Active)
49.2% Median Resp. Ratio (Dead)

Analysis

The responsive ratio measures the fraction of individual trials where the stimulus window has higher variance than the rest window. By chance, this value should hover around 50%.

Dead channels: The mean responsive ratio is 47.0% with a median of 49.2%, confirming that these channels behave as expected for noise-dominated signals—stimulus and rest windows are essentially interchangeable.

Active channels: The mean responsive ratio is 72.9%, well above the 50% chance level. This confirms that on a trial-by-trial basis, these channels consistently show increased energy during acoustic stimulation.

The correlation between broadband SNR and responsive ratio among active channels is moderately positive (Pearson r = 0.516, p = 0.034), confirming that higher-SNR channels tend to respond more consistently across trials.

Key Finding — Hypothesis Supported: Active channels show a responsive ratio significantly above 50%, confirming reliable trial-by-trial stimulus-evoked increases in signal energy. Dead channels sit right at chance level (~49%), behaving like pure noise. The responsive ratio thus serves as an independent validation of the SNR-based channel classification.

5. RQ4: Frequency Specificity (Tonotopic Tuning)

Does the SNR vary per channel depending on sound frequency, indicating true tonotopic neural tuning?

Results

0.837 Mean Tuning (Active)
0.090 Mean Tuning (Dead)
3.43 Max Tuning (Active)
1.36 Max Tuning (Dead)

Analysis

The tuning metric is the standard deviation of per-frequency SNR values across stimulus types within each channel. A high tuning metric indicates that a channel responds differentially to different acoustic frequencies—evidence of tonotopic organization.

Active channels have a mean tuning metric nearly 10× higher than dead channels (0.837 vs. 0.090). The standout channel is CG2D2E1 in sub-04_ses-01 RH with a tuning metric of 3.43, which also has the highest broadband SNR (1.54).

The correlation between broadband SNR and tuning metric among active channels is very strong (Pearson r = 0.869, p < 0.001), indicating that higher SNR channels tend to show more frequency-specific responses.

Key Finding — Hypothesis Supported: Active channels exhibit strong frequency-dependent SNR variation (high tuning metric), consistent with genuine tonotopic neural processing. Dead channels show flat, near-zero tuning—their SNR does not meaningfully change with stimulus frequency, consistent with systemic artifact or noise. The tight correlation between SNR and tuning (r = 0.87) suggests that channels with better signal quality also capture more frequency-specific neural information.

6. Diagnostic Plots

SNR Histogram

The distribution of broadband SNR across all 736 channels. The red dashed line marks the 0.5 threshold. The overwhelming concentration near zero is clearly visible, with only a thin tail extending past the threshold.

Top vs. Bottom ERP Comparison

Grand-average ERPs for the top 5 highest-SNR channels vs. the bottom 5 lowest-SNR channels. The top channels show clear, repeatable stimulus-evoked waveforms with large amplitude deflections. The bottom channels show flat, featureless traces—confirming that the SNR metric successfully separates channels with genuine neural responses from those dominated by noise.

7. Does SNR Predict Decoding Performance Across Baselines?

A frequency-decoding experiment was run on the same 41 sessions using 6 different baseline architectures (EEGNet, GRU, Linear, MLP, ShallowCNN, TemporalCNN). This section investigates whether the evoked-potential SNR and the power-ratio SNR are consistent predictors of downstream decoding performance regardless of model choice.

Correlation Results

Spearman rank correlations between SNR metrics and macro F1, computed separately for each baseline (N=41 sessions per baseline, 246 total observations):

Baseline Max Broadband SNR (ERP)
Spearman ρ (p)		 Max Tonotopic Tuning
Spearman ρ (p)		 Mean Power Ratio SNR
Spearman ρ (p)		 Mean Induced Power SNR
Spearman ρ (p)		 Max Habituation Index
Spearman ρ (p)
EEGNet 0.648 (4.6×10−6) 0.665 (2.1×10−6) 0.194 (0.223) −0.148 (0.357) 0.246 (0.120)
GRU 0.592 (4.5×10−5) 0.624 (1.3×10−5) −0.040 (0.803) −0.297 (0.060) 0.330 (0.035)
ShallowCNN 0.625 (1.2×10−5) 0.558 (1.5×10−4) 0.127 (0.429) −0.154 (0.337) 0.154 (0.337)
Linear 0.542 (2.5×10−4) 0.517 (5.4×10−4) 0.125 (0.435) −0.203 (0.204) −0.012 (0.942)
MLP 0.512 (6.2×10−4) 0.457 (2.7×10−3) 0.266 (0.093) 0.050 (0.758) 0.004 (0.982)
TemporalCNN 0.275 (0.082) 0.292 (0.064) 0.096 (0.550) 0.024 (0.881) −0.011 (0.944)
ALL (pooled, N=246) 0.478 (2.0×10−15) 0.480 (1.4×10−15) 0.116 (0.069) −0.107 (0.095) 0.119 (0.062)

Key Findings

Both Max Broadband SNR (ERP) and Max Tonotopic Tuning are strong, consistent predictors of decoding performance. Both evoked-potential metrics show significant Spearman correlations with F1 in 5 out of 6 baseline models (ρ = 0.51–0.67 for tuning; ρ = 0.51–0.65 for max SNR; all p < 0.001). The pooled correlations are nearly identical (ρ ≈ 0.48, p < 10−15), confirming that the evoked-potential signal quality reliably predicts performance regardless of model architecture.
Power Ratio SNR does NOT predict decoding performance. Despite revealing that 44.7% of channels carry stimulus-driven power (Section 11, RQ6), the Mean Power Ratio SNR fails to significantly predict F1 for any individual baseline (ρ = −0.04 to 0.27, all p > 0.05). This dissociation is critical: detecting any stimulus-driven power change is not the same as having frequency-discriminative neural responses that enable classification.
TemporalCNN is the exception. Neither SNR metric reaches significance for TemporalCNN (p = 0.06–0.08), though the trends are positive. This model may rely on different temporal features than those captured by the epoch-based SNR metrics.
Mean Induced Power SNR and Max Habituation Index do not predict decoding performance. Induced Power SNR is non-significant for all baselines (ρ = −0.30 to 0.05, all p > 0.05 except near-marginal for GRU). Max Habituation Index reaches significance only for GRU (ρ = 0.33, p = 0.035). This reinforces the finding that phase-locked, frequency-discriminative responses — not total stimulus power or temporal response dynamics — drive decoding success.

Diagnostic Plots

Conclusion

The evoked-potential SNR (both max channel SNR and tonotopic tuning) is a robust predictor of decoding success across architectures. Sessions with at least one high-SNR channel or strong frequency selectivity will consistently achieve higher F1 scores regardless of whether the decoder is a linear model, CNN, or RNN. The Power Ratio SNR, while useful for detecting the presence of stimulus-driven activity, does not predict the magnitude of decoding performance.

8. Is Session Performance Consistent Across Baselines?

Do some sessions always decode well (or poorly) regardless of model architecture, or does the relative ranking of sessions depend heavily on the specific baseline used?

Session Concordance Statistics

W = 0.747 Kendall’s W (concordance across 6 baselines)
ρ = 0.696 Mean pairwise Spearman rank correlation
CV = 0.44 Median coefficient of variation (F1 within session)

Kendall’s W = 0.747 indicates strong agreement in session rankings across the 6 baseline models (W = 1 would mean perfect agreement; W > 0.7 is generally considered strong concordance). Sessions that perform well with one model tend to perform well with all others.

The median CV of 0.44 shows that while relative rankings are preserved, the absolute F1 magnitude can vary substantially within a session across baselines. Some models extract more signal than others, but they largely agree on which sessions are the easiest and hardest.

Pairwise Baseline Agreement

Session Performance Heatmap

Conclusion

Session performance is highly consistent across baselines. With Kendall’s W = 0.747 and mean pairwise ρ = 0.70, the relative ranking of sessions is largely architecture-independent. Some sessions are intrinsically easier to decode due to their neural signal quality (high evoked SNR, strong tonotopic tuning), and this advantage persists regardless of whether the decoder is a linear model, CNN, or RNN.
Session-level variability dominates model-level variability. The variability in F1 driven by which session is being decoded is far larger than the variability introduced by model choice. This means that when evaluating new decoding methods, the choice of which sessions to include matters more than which model to use.
Practical implication: The SNR analysis (Section 7) can serve as a reliable a priori predictor of decoder-friendly sessions. Sessions with high max broadband SNR or strong tonotopic tuning will consistently produce good results across any reasonable architecture.

10. RQ5: Does Low-Frequency Filtering (1–70 Hz) Improve SNR?

Motivation: The original broadband filter (1–300 Hz) retains high-frequency components that may be dominated by noise (muscle artifacts, electrical interference) rather than neural signal. Since the high-gamma analysis (RQ2) revealed near-zero SNR above 70 Hz, we hypothesize that restricting the passband to 1–70 Hz could improve SNR by removing noise-dominated frequencies while preserving the evoked potentials that carry genuine auditory responses.

Hypothesis

Low-frequency filtering (1–70 Hz + 50 Hz notch) will yield higher channel-level SNR and responsive ratios compared to broadband filtering (1–300 Hz + 50 Hz notch), because high-frequency noise is removed while the dominant low-frequency evoked potentials are preserved.

Spearman ρ (BB resp vs LF resp) ρ = 0.9825 p < 10−300 Responsive ratios are highly correlated across filter bands
Spearman ρ (BB tuning vs LF tuning) ρ = 0.9939 p < 10−300 Tonotopic tuning metrics are nearly identical

Diagnostic Plots

SNR Distribution Comparison

Overlaid histograms showing the distribution of channel-level SNR under broadband (blue) and low-frequency (red) filtering.

Each dot represents one channel. Points above the diagonal indicate channels where low-frequency filtering yields higher SNR.

Comparison of active channel counts per session between broadband and low-frequency filtering (only sessions with any active channels shown).

Analysis

Low-frequency filtering provides a small but statistically significant SNR improvement. The Wilcoxon signed-rank test confirms that 1–70 Hz filtering yields significantly higher SNR than 1–300 Hz broadband (p = 1.06 × 10−52), with 78.9% of channels showing an increase. The effect is consistent across the entire SNR distribution.
Three additional channels cross the 0.5 SNR threshold with low-frequency filtering. Two channels in sub-05_ses-01 (SG2D1E7, SG2D1E11) show meaningful gains of +0.055–0.066 SNR, crossing from “Dead” to “Active.” A third borderline channel in sub-03_ses-04 (SG1D1E10) crosses by a narrow margin. No channels are lost in the transition.
The practical effect size is modest. Mean SNR improves by only +0.0015 across all channels, and the median gain is +0.0012. For channels already classified as active by broadband criteria, the mean SNR is slightly lower under LF filtering (−0.023), suggesting that some evoked energy in the 70–300 Hz range does contribute to SNR on already-strong channels.
Tonotopic tuning is marginally enhanced. Among active channels, mean tuning metric increases from 0.837 to 0.900 (+7.5%) under low-frequency filtering, consistent with cleaner frequency-specific ERPs when high-frequency noise is removed.
The two filter bands produce near-identical channel rankings. The Spearman rank correlation of 0.992 between BB and LF SNR means that low-frequency filtering does not fundamentally change which channels are considered “best” — it simply shifts the entire distribution upward slightly.

Conclusion

Verdict: Hypothesis Partially Supported
Low-frequency (1–70 Hz) filtering produces a statistically significant but practically small improvement in SNR compared to broadband (1–300 Hz). The improvement is sufficient to recover 3 borderline channels and marginally enhances tonotopic tuning, but does not fundamentally change the quality landscape of this dataset. The strongest argument for low-frequency filtering is that it provides these gains at no cost — zero channels are lost. For datasets where many channels cluster near the activity threshold, this small shift could be more impactful.

11. RQ6: Power Ratio SNR — Is Low Evoked SNR Caused by Phase-Locking Assumptions?

Motivation

The evoked-potential SNR used throughout this report (RQ1–RQ5) relies on a critical assumption: that neural responses to acoustic stimuli are phase-locked across trials. The numerator averages stimulus waveforms across all trials before computing variance, which acts as a matched filter for repeatable, time-locked activity. Any neural response that varies in latency, amplitude, or waveform shape from trial to trial will be attenuated or cancelled by this averaging.

With 97.7% of channels classified as “Dead” under the evoked SNR metric, a natural question arises: is the low evoked SNR a true reflection of absent neural responses, or is it an artifact of the phase-locking assumption? It is possible that channels carry real stimulus-driven activity that is induced (power changes without consistent phase) rather than evoked (phase-locked ERPs).

Hypothesis

H6: If neural responses are present but not precisely time-locked across trials, a Power Ratio SNR — which compares mean single-trial power during stimulus vs. rest without requiring phase consistency — should yield substantially higher SNR values than the evoked-potential metric. Specifically, we expect:
  1. Power Ratio SNR will be significantly higher than evoked SNR across all channels.
  2. A substantial fraction of “Dead” channels (by evoked criteria) will show Power Ratio > 1.0, indicating genuine stimulus-driven energy increases.
  3. Power Ratio SNR will correlate with responsive ratio (which is also phase-insensitive), but weakly with evoked SNR.

Method: Power Ratio SNR

The Power Ratio SNR is computed per channel c as:

SNRpower, c = [ (1/N) ∑i=1..N Var(Si,c(t)) ] / [ (1/N) ∑i=1..N Var(Ri,c(t)) ]

Unlike the evoked SNR, no trial-averaging is performed before computing variance. Each stimulus and rest epoch is measured individually, and then the per-trial variances are averaged. This means:

  • Power Ratio > 1.0: On average, individual stimulus epochs carry more total energy than matched rest epochs — regardless of whether the response waveform is consistent across trials.
  • Power Ratio ≈ 1.0: Stimulus and rest have equal power — no detectable energy increase.
  • Power Ratio < 1.0: Rest epochs have more energy than stimulus epochs (possibly due to desynchronisation or stimulus-induced suppression).

Analysis

The phase-locking assumption is the dominant factor driving low evoked SNR. The evoked SNR is 15× lower than the power ratio SNR on average. The Wilcoxon test confirms that the power ratio is higher for every single channel (stat = 0.0, p = 3.83 × 10−122). This is not simply a scale difference — the two metrics are essentially uncorrelated (ρ = 0.051, p = 0.17), meaning they measure fundamentally different properties of the signal.
Nearly half of all channels show stimulus-driven power increases. 329 of 736 channels (44.7%) have power ratio > 1.0, meaning that on individual trials, stimulus epochs carry more energy than rest epochs. This includes 313 channels classified as “Dead” by the evoked metric. These channels carry real stimulus-related information that the phase-locked analysis completely misses.
Power ratio SNR and responsive ratio are measuring the same underlying phenomenon. The near-perfect Spearman correlation of ρ = 0.898 between power ratio and responsive ratio confirms that both phase-insensitive metrics agree on which channels respond to stimulation. Meanwhile, the evoked SNR is essentially orthogonal to both (ρ = 0.051 with power ratio), reinforcing that the evoked metric selects specifically for phase-locked responses.
The power ratio is consistent across frequency bands. Broadband (0.973), high-gamma (0.987), and low-frequency (0.975) bands all show similar mean power ratios. Unlike the evoked SNR where high-gamma was nearly zero, the power ratio shows that even the high-gamma band carries modest stimulus-related power changes on many channels.
Sessions without “Active” channels still show stimulus-driven power. Several sessions with zero active channels (by evoked criteria) have mean power ratios above 1.0. For example, sub-04_ses-01 LH (mean power ratio 1.70) and sub-03_ses-01 LH (1.43) both contain channels with strong stimulus-driven power increases that are invisible to the evoked metric.

Conclusion

Verdict: Hypothesis Strongly Supported
The low evoked SNR observed throughout this dataset is substantially caused by the phase-locking assumption of the evoked-potential metric, not by an absence of neural responses. When assessed with a phase-insensitive power ratio, 44.7% of channels show stimulus power exceeding rest power (compared to only 2.3% classified as “Active” by evoked SNR). The two metrics are virtually uncorrelated, confirming that they capture different aspects of neural activity.

This has important implications for downstream decoding: models that can exploit non-phase-locked, trial-variable responses (e.g. deep learning on single-trial power features, time-frequency representations, or learned temporal alignments) may be able to extract useful information from channels that appear “dead” under the classical evoked-potential framework. The fact that many sessions achieve moderate decoding F1 scores despite having zero “Active” channels (see Sections 7–9) is consistent with this interpretation — the decoder is likely leveraging non-phase-locked stimulus-driven power changes that the evoked SNR completely discards.

12. RQ6 Addendum: Induced Power Decomposition

Motivation

The Power Ratio SNR established in RQ6 showed that 44.7% of channels carry stimulus-driven power that the evoked metric misses. But it does not distinguish why the power ratio is high. Total single-trial power can be decomposed into two orthogonal components:

  • Evoked power: Var(ERP) — the variance of the trial-averaged waveform, reflecting phase-locked responses.
  • Induced power: meani[Var(Si,c)] − Var(ERPc) — the residual single-trial variance after removing the phase-locked component.

If Hypothesis A is correct (neural responses are present but not phase-locked), then induced power should dominate total single-trial power, and the Induced SNR should be strongly correlated with Power Ratio SNR but uncorrelated with evoked SNR.

Method: Induced Power SNR

Induced_varc = meani[Var(Si,c(t))] − Var(ERPc(t))
Induced_SNRc = Induced_varc / meani[Var(Ri,c(t))]

Note that Power Ratio SNR = Evoked SNR + Induced SNR (since mean single-trial variance equals evoked variance plus induced variance). This decomposition tells us directly how much of the power ratio comes from phase-locked vs. non-phase-locked responses.

Results

0.909
Mean Induced SNR (all channels)
0.957
Median Induced SNR
0.064
Mean Evoked SNR (all channels)
0.973
Mean Power Ratio SNR (all channels)

Induced power overwhelmingly dominates total single-trial variance:

  • 735 / 736 channels (99.9%) have Induced SNR > Evoked SNR — virtually every channel’s stimulus response is dominated by non-phase-locked activity.
  • Spearman(ρ) between Induced SNR and Power Ratio SNR: 0.832 (p = 2.87 × 10−190) — the two metrics are strongly correlated, confirming that most of the power ratio comes from induced (non-phase-locked) power.
  • Spearman(ρ) between Induced SNR and Evoked SNR: −0.357 (p = 1.64 × 10−23) — the two are weakly anti-correlated, meaning that channels with strong induced responses tend to have weaker phase-locked ERPs.

The decomposition confirms the additive relationship: Power Ratio SNR (0.973) ≈ Evoked SNR (0.064) + Induced SNR (0.909). Induced power accounts for 93.4% of the total single-trial stimulus variance.

Interpretation

Induced power dominates: 93.4% of total single-trial stimulus variance comes from non-phase-locked activity. The weak anti-correlation with evoked SNR (ρ = −0.36) further suggests that channels with the strongest neural responses tend to respond with variable timing across trials, making them invisible to the ERP-based metric. This directly confirms Hypothesis A: the low evoked SNR is due to phase-locking failure, not absence of neural responses.

13. RQ7: Does Neural Habituation Explain Low ERP SNR?

Motivation

An alternative explanation for low evoked SNR (Hypothesis B): early trials may produce strong phase-locked ERPs that habituate (diminish) over the course of the session. If habituation is substantial, averaging across all trials would dilute strong early responses with flat late responses, yielding low overall evoked SNR.

Hypothesis

H7: If neural habituation is a significant factor:
  1. Evoked SNR computed from early trials (Q1) should be substantially higher than SNR from late trials (Q4).
  2. The Habituation Index (HI) should be positive for most channels.
  3. Cumulative ERP SNR should peak early and decline as more trials are added.

Methods

Quartile SNR Analysis

Trials are split chronologically into four equal quartiles (Q1 = earliest 25%, Q4 = latest 25%). Evoked SNR is computed independently for each quartile:

SNRq,c = Var(ERPq,c) / meani∈Qq[Var(Ri,c)]

Habituation Index (HI)

HIc = (SNRearly,c − SNRlate,c) / (SNRearly,c + SNRlate,c + ε)
  • HI > 0: Habituation (early trials stronger)
  • HI < 0: Sensitization (late trials stronger)
  • HI ≈ 0: Stable response

Cumulative ERP SNR

ERP SNR is computed using the first K trials, for K = 5, 10, 15, …, N. If habituation is present, SNR should peak at a small K and decline as flat late trials dilute the average.

Results

0.200
Mean Habituation Index
0.249
Median Habituation Index
0.103
Mean Q1 SNR (earliest 25%)
0.065
Mean Q4 SNR (latest 25%)
  • 461 / 736 channels (62.6%) have HI > 0.1 — a majority of channels show meaningful habituation (early trials stronger than late).
  • 194 / 736 channels (26.4%) have HI < −0.1 — a substantial minority show sensitization (late trials stronger than early).
  • Wilcoxon signed-rank test (Q1 vs Q4): stat = 73,523, p = 5.31 × 10−27 — Q1 SNR is significantly higher than Q4 SNR across channels.
  • Spearman(ρ) between HI and Evoked SNR: 0.238 (p = 6.06 × 10−11) — channels with higher evoked SNR tend to show slightly more habituation, suggesting that the strongest responders also habituate.

Diagnostic Plots

Interpretation

Both mechanisms contribute: The median HI of 0.249 and the highly significant Q1 vs Q4 difference (p = 5.31 × 10−27) confirm that neural habituation is a real and measurable effect. Early trials produce evoked SNR that is ~59% higher than late trials (0.103 vs 0.065). However, even Q1 SNR (0.103) remains far below the 0.5 “Active” threshold, indicating that habituation alone does not explain the low evoked SNR — most of the deficit comes from non-phase-locking (Hypothesis A, confirmed in Section 12).
Habituation is a secondary but significant factor (Hypothesis B partially supported). The 62.6% of channels with HI > 0.1 shows systematic response diminishment over the session. This is partially offset by the 26.4% of channels showing sensitization (HI < −0.1). The weak positive correlation between HI and evoked SNR (ρ = 0.238) suggests that the best-responding channels are also the most prone to habituation — the strongest signals fade the fastest.
Practical implication: Using early-session trials only (e.g., first quartile) would yield ~59% higher evoked SNR, though this comes at the cost of reduced trial count. Given that Hypothesis A dominates, single-trial analysis methods (which do not require phase-locking) are still the recommended strategy.

14. Conclusions

Summary of Findings

Research Question Hypothesis Outcome
RQ1: Channel & Session SNR Evoked-potential SNR flags dead channels; averaging active channels gives a reliable session score Supported — The SNR metric clearly separates 17 active channels from 719 dead channels. However, only 5/41 sessions have any active channels, limiting the utility of session-level aggregation.
RQ2: High-Gamma Sensitivity High-gamma filtering isolates neural signals better than broadband Not Supported — High-gamma SNR is extremely low for all channels. Evoked responses in this dataset are carried primarily by low-frequency components, not high-gamma power.
RQ3: Responsive Ratio Active channels show stimulus energy increase above 50% chance Supported — Active channels average 72.9% responsive ratio vs. 47.0% for dead channels, independently validating the SNR classification.
RQ4: Tonotopic Tuning SNR varies by stimulus frequency on responsive channels Supported — Active channels show ~10× higher tuning metrics than dead channels, with strong frequency-specific responses.
RQ5: Low-Frequency Filtering 1–70 Hz filtering improves SNR by removing high-frequency noise Partially Supported — Statistically significant but small SNR improvement (Wilcoxon p = 1.06 × 10−52). Three channels recovered, zero lost. Tonotopic tuning marginally enhanced (+7.5%). Practical effect is modest.
RQ6: Power Ratio SNR Low evoked SNR is caused by phase-locking assumption; power ratio reveals actual signal Strongly Supported — Power ratio SNR is 15× higher than evoked SNR on average. 44.7% of channels show power ratio > 1.0 (stimulus power exceeds rest). 313 “Dead” channels have power ratio > 1.0. The two metrics are uncorrelated (ρ = 0.051), capturing fundamentally different aspects of neural activity.
RQ6 Addendum: Induced Power Induced (non-phase-locked) power dominates total single-trial power Strongly Supported — Induced power accounts for 93.4% of total single-trial variance (Induced SNR = 0.909 vs Evoked SNR = 0.064). 99.9% of channels have Induced > Evoked. Induced SNR strongly correlates with Power Ratio SNR (ρ = 0.832) and is weakly anti-correlated with Evoked SNR (ρ = −0.357), confirming Hypothesis A.
RQ7: Habituation Strong early ERPs are diluted by flat late trials during averaging Partially Supported — Median HI = 0.249; Q1 SNR is 59% higher than Q4 SNR (p = 5.31 × 10−27). 62.6% of channels habituate. However, even Q1 SNR (0.103) remains below the Active threshold (0.5), so habituation is secondary to non-phase-locking (Hypothesis A).
Section 7: SNR vs. F1 (multi-baseline) SNR predicts decoding performance regardless of model architecture Strongly Supported — Both Max Broadband SNR (ERP) and Max Tonotopic Tuning correlate significantly with F1 in 5/6 baselines (ρ = 0.51–0.67). Power Ratio SNR does not predict performance.
Section 8: Session consistency Session quality dominates over model choice Strongly Supported — Session rankings are highly consistent across baselines (Kendall’s W = 0.747, mean pairwise ρ = 0.70). Sessions with high SNR decode well regardless of architecture.

Implications

1. Most channels lack phase-locked evoked potentials, but many carry stimulus-driven power changes. While 97.7% of channels are classified as “Dead” by the evoked-potential SNR, 44.7% of channels show power ratio > 1.0, indicating genuine stimulus-driven energy increases that are not phase-locked. The dataset’s signal quality is substantially better than the evoked metric alone suggests.
2. The evoked-potential SNR selects specifically for phase-locked responses. It effectively separates channels with reliable ERPs from those without, correlates with trial-by-trial reliability and tonotopic tuning, and predicts downstream decoding performance. However, it is blind to induced (non-phase-locked) neural activity.
3. Power ratio SNR and responsive ratio provide complementary, phase-insensitive quality assessment. These two metrics are strongly correlated with each other (ρ = 0.898) and capture stimulus-driven energy changes regardless of phase consistency. They reveal neural responsiveness that the evoked metric completely misses.
4. Max Broadband SNR and Tonotopic Tuning are equally strong, consistent predictors of decoding success. Both evoked-potential metrics correlate significantly with F1 across 5 of 6 tested baseline models (max SNR: ρ = 0.51–0.65; tuning: ρ = 0.46–0.67). Power Ratio SNR does not predict performance. The distinction matters: detecting any stimulus-driven power is not the same as having discriminative neural responses.
5. Session quality dominates model choice in determining performance. With Kendall’s W = 0.747 across 6 baselines, the relative ranking of sessions is highly stable regardless of model architecture. The choice of which sessions to include matters more than which model to train.
6. Low-frequency filtering (1–70 Hz) is a safe default over broadband. It yields a small but consistent SNR improvement with zero channel loss, recovers borderline channels, and marginally improves tonotopic tuning. The gains are modest but come at no cost.
7. Decoding models should exploit non-phase-locked responses. The disconnect between evoked SNR (97.7% dead) and power ratio SNR (44.7% above parity) explains why many sessions with zero “Active” channels still achieve moderate decoding F1 scores. Models that operate on single-trial features (power, time-frequency, or learned representations) rather than trial-averaged ERPs can access stimulus information that is invisible to classical evoked-potential analysis. This is a strong argument for deep learning approaches that learn temporal alignments rather than assuming fixed phase locking.
8. Induced (non-phase-locked) power is the dominant component of stimulus-driven activity. The induced power decomposition (Section 12) shows that 93.4% of single-trial stimulus variance is non-phase-locked. 99.9% of channels have Induced SNR > Evoked SNR, and channels with the strongest induced responses tend to have weaker phase-locked ERPs (ρ = −0.36). This provides a mechanistic explanation for the decoding-SNR paradox: models succeed because they learn from trial-varying neural activity patterns, not from the tiny phase-locked component.
9. Neural habituation is real but secondary to non-phase-locking. The habituation analysis (Section 13) reveals that 62.6% of channels habituate (HI > 0.1) and early-trial SNR is 59% higher than late-trial SNR. However, even peak early-trial SNR (0.103) remains well below the Active threshold (0.5). Habituation contributes to low evoked SNR but is not the primary cause — non-phase-locking (Hypothesis A) accounts for the vast majority of the deficit.
